title: How Class Action Lawsuits Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how class action lawsuits work: the idea of pooling many similarly harmed people into one civil suit, the representative (lead) plaintiff and class counsel, the history from medieval English courts and equity courts through Rule 48 and Rule 23 (1966) and the Class Action Fairness Act of 2005, the certification requirement (Dukes v. Walmart), notice and opt-out, judges setting attorney fees and distributing settlements, and the advantages and criticisms, including coupon settlements, the Subway foot-long case, the Vitamin Water suit, and large settlements like tobacco, BP, and Volkswagen. The episode closes with a listener mail about a penny farthing sighting.

entities.name: Center for Science in the Public Interest

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to class actions
segments.summary: Hosts chat about movies and David Crosby, then introduce class action lawsuits as a way for many people with similar harms to pool resources against a large defendant, and explain the representative plaintiff and class counsel roles.

segments.title: History: English courts, equity courts, and early group suits
segments.summary: The hosts trace common law from England and the Vikings, describe group complaints in early English courts, and explain equity courts and how they handled non-monetary remedies. They note early disputes over whether absent people were bound by decisions.

segments.title: Rule 48, Rule 23, and the Class Action Fairness Act
segments.summary: The hosts describe the development of Rule 48 and Rule 23 in 1966, which bound class members to decisions unless they opted out, the 1937 federal rules, and the Class Action Fairness Act of 2005 that moved large or diverse cases to federal court.

segments.title: Certification, notice, opt-out, and class counsel
segments.summary: The hosts explain certification requirements using a hypothetical oil spill and the Dukes v. Walmart case, where the Supreme Court rejected a class of 1.5 million women. They cover class definition, notice to members, opt-out rights, and judges choosing class counsel and approving distribution and fees.

segments.title: Advantages of class actions
segments.summary: The hosts list advantages: pooled resources against costly lawsuits, higher-caliber lawyers, avoiding a first-come-first-served race to a defendant's assets, and settlements that end long-running problems and generate press.

segments.title: Criticisms, coupon settlements, and famous cases
segments.summary: The hosts discuss criticisms such as lawyers receiving large fees while members get little, coupon settlements (Subway foot-long, Vitamin Water sugar suit), and large settlements including tobacco, BP, Volkswagen, the Boy Scouts abuse case, and the silicone breast implant litigation.

segments.title: Listener mail: penny farthing coincidence
segments.summary: A listener named Sean writes in about seeing a penny farthing bicycle in his Colorado town after an earlier episode mentioned one.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and invite listener emails.
